entries.clue: In this way, vacuous business breaks down (4)

indicatorNotes.vacuous: Something vacuous is empty in the middle, so the word beside it keeps only the letters at its two ends.

blocks.note: 'do it in this way' and 'do it so' are the same sentence
the first and last letters of the word, the middle hollowed out

annotation.surface: A company with nothing inside it collapsing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Breaks down' looks like the fate of the business and is the definition instead — something a person does, not a firm. 'Vacuous' is the setter's standing request for a word's outside letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who breaks down in front of you has lost composure and is weeping aloud, which is what the answer names.

entries.clue: Reports of flying objects (5,5)

blocks.note: read first as written accounts, the sightings people file with the authorities; read again as the other kind of report, the bang a gun or a firework makes
the surface wants the unidentified sort; the setter means ordinary aircraft, the ones fast enough to pass the speed of sound

annotation.surface: UFO sightings being written up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reports of flying objects' is UFO language start to finish, and the whole trap is the second sense of report: a bang. An aircraft crossing the sound barrier drags a pressure wave behind it, heard on the ground as a double crack.
annotation.definitionFit: The clue reads straight once 'report' means a bang: the noise an aircraft makes as it goes supersonic is exactly a report of a flying object.

entries.clue: PM stands for Polar Mammals? No, their relatives (5,5)

blocks.note: the initials are the standing shorthand for Prime Minister, and Gordon Brown held the job from 2007 to 2010
'I can't stand it' and 'I can't bear it' are the same complaint

annotation.surface: A quibble over what the letters PM are short for.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue offers its own false expansion of the initials — Polar Mammals — and the ones that matter are political. The white bears of the Arctic split from the answer's species recently enough that the two still interbreed.
annotation.definitionFit: Polar bears descend from the shaggy inland species the answer names, and the two are close enough to produce cubs together, so 'relatives' is literal zoology.

entries.clue: The northern newspaper twice backing stand-up that's funny some of the time (10)

indicatorNotes.twice: 'Twice' asks for the job beside it to be done two times over, so two different papers are named one after the other.

blocks.note: in northern English speech 'the' shrinks to a clipped t', as in 'up t'road'
a rag is the dismissive word for a paper
the i is a British daily, launched as a compact offshoot of the Independent
a stand-up is someone who tells jokes at a microphone

annotation.surface: A northern comedian with two papers behind him, raising a laugh now and then.
annotation.walkthrough: Two entirely different newspapers answer the same word, which is what 'twice' is there to tell you: the slang one and the one that is a single letter. A tragicomedy keeps both masks on stage at once.
annotation.definitionFit: A story that mixes grief with comedy raises its laughs only in patches, which is what 'some of the time' is measuring.

entries.clue: Billionaire is sued - mostly ignored - we've seen this before (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a remark rather than a noun: what it describes is a record or a book put out a second time, and the clue names it by the flicker of recognition it produces instead of by a synonym.

indicatorNotes.mostly ignored: If most of what is in front of you is to be ignored, what survives is a short run taken in the order it already lies.

blocks.note: the run starts near the end of the long first word and carries straight on through the next two, stopping a letter short of the finish

annotation.surface: A very rich man being taken to court while nobody pays much attention.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mostly ignored' is doing the work of 'hidden in', and it is honest about it — in a clue like this most of the letters really are discarded. The two word-joins inside the run are what keep it out of sight.
annotation.definitionFit: Something put out a second time — a record repressed, a paperback reprinted — arrives with the reader's sense of having met it already.

entries.clue: Slate in recess in Victorian street feature (3,4)

indicatorNotes.in: Putting one word in another sets it bodily inside, so the letters named first go within the letters named next.

blocks.note: a recess in a wall is a gap left in it
to slate a play is to slam it — both mean to review it savagely

annotation.surface: A piece of slate tucked into an alcove in an old street.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Slate' is the critics' verb here, not the roofing material the surface offers. British streets were lit by burning gas from the 1810s until electricity took over, so a fluted post with a flame in a glass box dates a scene at a glance.
annotation.definitionFit: The lit post on a pavement is the stock signal for a nineteenth-century street, which is the period 'Victorian' names.

entries.clue: Supporter of wicked things (11)

blocks.note: read as a backer, someone who champions a cause; read again as a thing that physically holds something up
read as evil deeds, and then as objects that have wicks in them

annotation.surface: Somebody who champions evil.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wicked' is being used as though it were the adjective from 'wick', which the spelling very nearly supports and the dictionary does not. The branched holder it describes stands several candles up at once, which is why the plural matters.
annotation.definitionFit: Read the second way the clue is literal: the branched holder's whole job is to carry things with wicks in them.

entries.clue: Like men in armour, you said? (4)

indicatorNotes.you said: 'You said' points at speech rather than spelling, so the word beside it is to be heard and then written down some other way.

blocks.note: the interlinked metal rings knights fought in are mail, as in chain mail

annotation.surface: Knights in armour, described as manly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In armour' looks like scenery attached to the men and is the entire wordplay. Chain mail takes its name from the French for a mesh and has nothing to do with the post.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Like men' asks for the adjective that sorts a person or an animal onto the men's side of the divide.

entries.clue: Having a bag sent up in Spanish home (4)

indicatorNotes.sent up: Sending something up moves it from the bottom towards the top, so in a down entry the letters beside it are read upwards.

blocks.note: a bag is a sac, and with its 'a' kept in front the four letters are then read back up the column

annotation.surface: A guest having luggage carried up to the room.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sent up' is hotel service on the surface and a turning instruction in the clue, and 'up' is the right word for it only because this entry runs down the grid. The word wanted is the ordinary Spanish one for a house.
annotation.definitionFit: It is the everyday Spanish word for a house, borrowed into English on the signs of villas and restaurants.

entries.clue: Two refusals, one rejected in time (4)

indicatorNotes.rejected: To reject something is to throw it back, and a short word thrown back is read from its last letter to its first.

blocks.note: the plainest word of refusal there is, and the clue asks for a pair of them
the second of that pair, turned round

annotation.surface: Two rejections, one of which is itself turned down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One' counts the refusals rather than joining in as a letter of its own, which is the only real trap. 'In time' reads as an idiom and is a link word with the definition behind it.
annotation.definitionFit: Twelve o'clock in the middle of the day is one particular point on the clock, so the definition names the class the answer sits in.

entries.clue: Attacks fireplaces in most popular songs (3,7)

blocks.note: to attack somebody is to hit them, and the verb takes the same -s
an ingle is an open hearth fire, a word that survives in 'inglenook'

annotation.surface: Fireplaces coming under attack in the nation's favourite songs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ingle' is the crossword word for a hearth and is worth learning once, because it comes back. The join between the chunks falls one letter inside the second word of the answer, which is what hides the seam.
annotation.definitionFit: The records that reach the charts as singles are the songs a listening public has actually made popular.

entries.clue: Small amount of money to remain mellow where the action is (6,5)

blocks.note: the hundredth of a dollar or a euro, the smallest coin most people handle
what rests stays put — 'the others remained' and 'the others rested' both leave them where they were
wine and cheese mellow as they age, so the two verbs swap

annotation.surface: Advice to hang on to a small sum and take things gently.
annotation.walkthrough: All three chunks are ordinary words pulling their weight, and both seams fall inside the answer's words rather than between them. An actor standing at the middle of the boards is the one the audience must look at, which is how the phrase came to mean prominence.
annotation.definitionFit: The middle of the acting area is where a director puts whatever matters most, so the phrase has come to mean the focus of attention.

entries.clue: Raised alarm - raider - one on the boat (4,7)

indicatorNotes.Raised: To raise a rumpus is to stir one up, and letters stirred up do not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: eleven letters across the two words, taken as they stand before the shuffle

annotation.surface: A break-in setting off the alarm.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Raised' reads as raising the alarm and is the shuffling instruction, which is why the dashes are there chopping the sentence into pieces. Despite the name, a rear admiral is the junior of the navy's flag ranks, below a vice admiral.
annotation.definitionFit: The rank is a naval one, so the man holding it is aboard ship — the definition names him by where he stands rather than by what he commands.

entries.clue: Octet of which we're a member - performing this suite? (3,7)

annotation.definition: Octet of which we're a member

blocks.clueFragment: Octet of which we're a member
blocks.note: read as astronomy: eight bodies going round the sun, the third of them the one under your feet
read as a concert programme instead — Holst's orchestral work, whose movements are named for those same bodies

annotation.surface: An orchestra playing a suite that the audience somehow belongs to.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Octet' offers a group of eight musicians and means something in the sky. Holst's suite has only seven movements, leaving out the very body the clue says we live on, and the count of eight is itself only settled since Pluto was demoted in 2006.
annotation.definitionFit: Earth is one of the eight bodies orbiting our sun, and Holst's orchestral suite of 1916 is named for that same set.

entries.clue: In Derby, 'agers' whimsically described as such? (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition points instead of naming: 'such' refers back to the clue's own coined word for people who are ageing, so the answer is the label being proposed for them rather than a synonym of anything in the clue.

indicatorNotes.whimsically: A whimsical arrangement is a fanciful one, made for fun rather than sense, so the letters beside it are resettled as the setter pleases.

blocks.note: ten letters across the city and the coined word beside it, taken as they stand before the shuffle

annotation.surface: A joke about what the ageing residents of Derby get called.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'agers' concede that it is not a word, which is the tell that it is raw material. Derby is a city in the East Midlands and is here for its letters, not for anything the answer has to do with the place.
annotation.definitionFit: Old men are named for the colour their beards turn, and the question mark concedes that the label is a playful one.

entries.clue: Not young enough? That's excessive! (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The two halves take the word different ways: one is the unhyphenated adjective for somebody past a limit, the other the noun for a surplus, which is why the second reads as an exclamation rather than as a synonym.

blocks.note: read as a complaint about somebody turned away for having passed the age limit
read again as a protest about quantity: more of something has turned up than was asked for

annotation.surface: Somebody rejected on age, objecting that the rule goes too far.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses want different stresses — over age, and an overage — and it is the single spelling that lets the clue hold both. Hauliers and retailers use the noun for the amount by which a delivery exceeds its order.
annotation.definitionFit: One sense puts a person beyond the age a rule allows; the other is the surplus left when a quantity comes in above its estimate.

entries.clue: Trespasser; thief; one getting into hot water? (7)

blocks.note: read as the countryside offence — taking game or fish off land belonging to somebody else, which is both charges at once
read as the kitchen verb instead: an egg slid into a pan of water just off the boil, and the person doing it named for the method

annotation.surface: A list of offences ending with somebody in trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In hot water' is the idiom for being in trouble, which is where the surface sends you, and the kitchen is where the clue means. One word covers the man with the net at midnight and the cook with the pan at breakfast.
annotation.definitionFit: Taking game off another's land is trespass and theft at once; in the kitchen the same word means cooking gently in water just off the boil.

entries.clue: Though always tailed, she's never seen (7)

annotation.definition: Though always tailed, she's never seen

blocks.note: read as somebody under constant surveillance, followed everywhere by a detective; read again as a body that ends in a fish's tail
read as the reason the surveillance keeps failing, and as the plain fact about a creature nobody has ever produced

annotation.surface: A woman under permanent surveillance who still manages never to be spotted.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tailed' is the hinge: police work in one sense, anatomy in the other, and the sentence runs smoothly either way. Sailors' sightings were most likely manatees, which is how the myth kept being confirmed.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight the clue describes a creature who is fish below the waist and has never been produced for inspection, which is the whole of what the word means.

entries.clue: After bolting candy, I'm energetic (7)

indicatorNotes.bolting: Food that is bolted goes down in a rush without being taken in any order, so the letters beside it come out rearranged.

blocks.note: seven letters across the sweet and the contraction beside it, taken as they stand before the shuffle

annotation.surface: A sugar rush reported from the inside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I'm' looks like the speaker reporting on themselves and is two of the letters, which is the move to spot. 'Bolting' is rarer than 'downing' or 'wolfing' as a shuffling word and does exactly the same job.
annotation.definitionFit: The word describes a person full of drive and forward motion, which is energy in action rather than energy in reserve.

entries.clue: Decline the World Cup, for example (7)

blocks.note: naming an instance asks for 'a' one of them, and that indefinite article is part of what gets written down
the gold statuette handed to football's world champions is one specimen of the class

annotation.surface: A team turning down the World Cup.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Decline' is the verb for refusing on the surface and the verb for wasting away in the definition, and nothing else in the clue moves at all. Seeing the answer as two words is the whole of the trick.
annotation.definitionFit: Muscle left unused wastes away, and that slow wasting is what 'decline' names as a verb.

entries.clue: Selection from Carmen I adapted somewhere in Asia (7)

indicatorNotes.Selection from: A selection from something is a piece lifted out of it whole, so a run of letters is to be taken out of the words that follow.

blocks.note: the run starts one letter into the opera's name and carries on straight across both word-joins

annotation.surface: An arrangement of numbers from Bizet's opera, staged somewhere out east.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Selection from Carmen' promises an aria and 'adapted' promises a shuffle; both are decoys for letters already lying in order. The italics mark the word as a title, which is the setter's only nudge that it is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: The country south of the Caucasus mountains is counted as part of western Asia, which is as precise as the definition asks for.

entries.clue: Small and quiet, carry on for scant remuneration (7,4)

blocks.note: a mini skirt or a mini break is a small one, and the prefix stands on its own
to keep mum is to say nothing
a war or a campaign is waged, which is to carry it on

annotation.surface: Advice to stay small and quiet and put up with poor pay.
annotation.walkthrough: Three separate words hand over three chunks and none of them is padding, so the sentence is built entirely out of its own wordplay. Britain's statutory floor on hourly pay has been set and revised annually since 1999.
annotation.definitionFit: The legal floor on hourly pay is as little as an employer may lawfully hand over, which is remuneration at its most scant.

entries.clue: Snake in hurricane? (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The second definition points rather than names: what a hurricane consists of is the answer, not what a hurricane is, and the question mark is the setter owning that looseness.

blocks.note: read as the verb: a lane that snakes bends one way and then the other
read as a noun instead, and said with a different vowel — the moving air a hurricane is made of

annotation.surface: A snake caught out in a hurricane.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses are spelt alike and said differently, one rhyming with 'find' and the other with 'pinned', and that mismatch is the joke. A hurricane is defined by speed: force 12, anything above 73mph.
annotation.definitionFit: A lane that snakes bends one way then the other, which is the answer's verb; and a hurricane is nothing but air moving very fast, which is its noun.

entries.clue: A small fellow, but enthralling - Everyman? Hardly (2,2)

indicatorNotes.enthralling: To enthral somebody is to hold them captive, so what is named next is held inside the letters already assembled.

blocks.note: the article taken as the single letter it is
the standard abbreviation on a clothing label
the standing abbreviation, as in Fellow of the Royal Society
the setter signs himself Everyman, so when he turns up in his own clue he is the first person

annotation.surface: A little chap who is nonetheless captivating company.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Everyman' is the setter's own name and, as in most of his puzzles, it means the first person singular. The phrase it builds is a flat refusal dressed up as a hypothetical, which is why the clue calls it hardly.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are dismissals: the reply says the thing just suggested is so unlikely it is not worth entertaining.

entries.clue: Viola perhaps prepared nutriments (10)

indicatorNotes.prepared: Food that has been prepared has been cut about and recombined, so the letters beside it arrive in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: ten letters of a formal word for foodstuffs, taken as they stand before the shuffle

annotation.surface: Viola in the kitchen, getting the food ready.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Viola' sits at the front of the clue so its capital proves nothing, and the girl's name and the alto fiddle are equally available. 'Perhaps' is the marker that one example is standing in for its whole class.
annotation.definitionFit: A viola is one of the string family, so naming it with 'perhaps' asks for the general word for a thing you play.

entries.clue: On hearing where you're seated in theatre, a show of sorrow (4)

indicatorNotes.On hearing: What you hear is a sound rather than a spelling, so the words beside it are to be said aloud and then written down another way.

blocks.note: theatre seats are banked in levels one above another, and each level is a tier

annotation.surface: Being told your seat number in a theatre and welling up.
annotation.walkthrough: Only one sense of the answer sounds like that: the ripping sense rhymes with 'bare' instead, and the clue quietly depends on your picking the right one. British theatres sell their tiers under names like the circle and the gods.
annotation.definitionFit: A single drop rolling down a cheek is the visible sign that somebody is upset, which is what 'a show of sorrow' asks for.

entries.clue: Endless fateful cold, shivering? You need this (6,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a recommendation rather than a synonym: the clue's freezing weather is the occasion and the answer is the garment that meets it, so no noun in the clue means what the answer means.

indicatorNotes.Endless: Something endless has had its end taken off, so the word beside it gives up its final letter before anything else is done to it.
indicatorNotes.shivering: A shiver runs through a thing and leaves nothing steady, so the letters beside it will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: six of the word's seven letters, the last one docked
four more letters, taken as they stand before the shuffle

annotation.surface: A grim spell of freezing weather that leaves you shaking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cold, shivering' reads as one unbroken description of the weather and is two separate jobs: the first word is raw material, the second is the instruction. The hooded coat with toggles and rope loops was Royal Navy issue long before it was student uniform.
annotation.definitionFit: The heavy hooded wool coat fastened with toggles is what you reach for when it is cold enough to shiver.

entries.clue: Goddess exists; you can say that again (4)

indicatorNotes.you can say that again: The stock way of agreeing hard with somebody is to invite them to repeat themselves, so the short word just given is written out a second time.

blocks.note: the third person of the verb 'to be', the two letters you write when you say a thing exists
the same two letters set down a second time, at the invitation of the phrase that follows

annotation.surface: Emphatic agreement that a goddess is real.
annotation.walkthrough: 'You can say that again' is the clue's only instruction and reads as pure conversation, which is exactly what hides it. The Egyptian goddess of magic also gave her name to the Thames where it runs through Oxford.
annotation.definitionFit: The Egyptian goddess of magic and motherhood, wife of Osiris and mother of Horus, is among the best known of that pantheon.
